None:\n119\t        if abs(val) > 1e-15:\n120\t            rows.append(ii)\n121\t            cols.append(jj)\n122\t            data.append(val)\n123\t\n124\t    for i in range(nx):\n125\t        for j in range(ny):\n126\t            # Cell dimensions\n127\t            dx_w = dx[i - 1] if i > 0 else dx[0]\n128\t            dx_e = dx[i] if i < nx - 1 else dx[-1]\n129\t            dy_s = dy[j - 1] if j > 0 else dy[0]\n130\t            dy_n = dy[j] if j < ny - 1 else dy[-1]\n131\t\n132\t            # ε at cell center\n133\t            eps_c = max(epsilon_zz(x[i], y[j]), 1e-10)\n134\t\n135\t        - 2.0 / (dy_s * (dy_s + dy_n))\n145\t                - 2.0 / (dy_n * (dy_s + dy_n))\n146\t                + k0**2 * eps_c\n147\t            )\n148\t\n149\t            idx = i * ny +  # For simplicity, we implement BCs by modifying the diagonal\n156\t            # and neighbor coefficients at the boundary\n157\t\n158\t            if i == 0:  # West\n159\t                # Ez at Dirichlet\n167\t                    diag += 2.0 / (dx_e * (dx_w + dx_e))\n168\t\n169\t            if j == 0:  # South\n170\t                if bc_south == 0:  # Dirichlet\n171\t                    diag += 2.0 / (dy_s * (dy_s + dy_n))\n172\t\n173\t            if j == ny - 1:  # North\n174\t                if bc_north == 0:  # Dirichlet\n175\t                    diag += 2.0 / (dy_n * (dy_s + dy_n))\n176\t\n177\t            _add(idx, idx, diag)\n178\t\n179\t            # Neighbor contributions\n180\t            if i > 0:\n181\t                _add(idx, (i - 1) * ny + j, 2.0 / (dx_w * (dx_w + dx_e)))\n182\t            if i < nx - 1:\n183\t                _add(idx, (i + 1) * ny + j, 2.0 / (dx_e * (dx_w + dx_e)))\n184\t            if j > 0:\n185\t                _add(idx, i * ny + (j - 1), 2.0 / (dy_s * (dy_s + dy_n)))\n186\t            if j < ny - 1:\n187\t                _add(idx, i * ny + (j + 1), 2.0 / (dy_n * (dy_s + dy_n)))\n188\t\n189\t    A = sparse.csc_matrix((data, (rows, \"sparse.csc_matrix | sparse.csr_matrix\":\n201\t    \"\"\"Assemble the sparse FD matrix for the vector mode problem.\n202\t\n203\t    For the general anisotropic case, we solve the full 2-component\n204\t    vector eigenvalue problem using the Yee-grid curl-curl operator.\n205\t\n206\t    Args:\n207\t        x: Cell-center x coordinates\n208\t        y: Cell-center y _map_boundary_condition(boundaries[3])\n232\t\n233\t    N = nx * ny\n234\t    rows: list[int] = []\n235\t    cols: list[int] = []\n236\t    data: list[float] = []\n237\t\n238\t    def _add(ii: int, safe_eps(f):\n245\t        return max(abs(f), 1e-10)\n246\t\n247\t    for i in range(nx):\n248\t        for j in range(ny):\n249\t            dx_w = dx[i - 1] if i > 0 else dx[0]\n250\t            dx_e = dx[i] if i < nx - 1 else dx[-1]\n251\t            dy_s = dy[j - 1] if j > 0 else dy[0]\n252\t            dy_n = dy[j] if j < ny - 1 else dy[-1]\n253\t\n254\t            eps_xx, eps_xy, eps_yx, eps_yy, eps_zz = epsilon(x[i], y[j])\n255\t            eps_xx = safe_eps(eps_xx)\n256\t            eps_yy = safe_eps(eps_yy)\n257\t            det_eps = eps_xx * eps_yy - eps_xy * eps_yx\n258\t\n259\t            # Get neighbor eps for averaging\n260\t            eps_xx_w = eps_xx\n261\t            eps_xx_e = eps_xx\n262\t            eps_yy_w = eps_yy\n263\t            eps_yy_e = eps_yy\n264\t            eps_xx_s = eps_xx\n265\t            eps_xx_n = eps_xx\n266\t            eps_yy_s = eps_yy\n267\t            eps_yy_n = eps_yy\n268\t\n269\t            if i > 0:\n270\t                eww, _, _, epsilon(x[i], y[j - 1])\n279\t                eps_xx_s = safe_eps(ews)\n280\t                eps_yy_s = safe_eps(eys)\n281\t            if j < ny - 1:\n282\t                ewn, _, _, eyn, _ = epsilon(x[i], y[j + 1])\n283\t                eps_xx_n = safe_eps(ewn)\n284\t                eps_yy_n = safe_eps(eyn)\n285\t\n286\t            # === Simplified curl-curl discretization ===\n287\t            # For the 2D cross-section, the curl-curl operator gives:\n288\t            # ∇ × (μ⁻¹ ∇ × H) = β² H in the transverse plane\n289\t            # For μ = μ₀ (vacuum), we need:\n290\t            # [1/εxx d²/dx² + 1/εyy d²/dy²] Hx = -β² Hx  [along x]\n291\t            # [1/εyy d²/dy² + 1/εxx d²/dx²] Hy = -β² Hy  [along y]\n292\t            #\n293\t            # Rearranging: -[1/εxx d²/dx² + 1/εyy d²/dy²] Hx = β² Hx\n294\t            #\n295\t            # This gives a NEGATIVE-DEFINITE operator whose eigenvalues are β² > 0.\n296\t            #\n297\t            # The FD discretization (1/εxx_e + 1/εxx_w)/(2*dx²) + (1/εyy_n + 1/εyy_s)/(2*dy²) - k₀²\n302\t            axxp = (\n303\t                (1.0 / eps_xx_e + 1.0 / eps_xx_w) / (2.0 * dx_e * dx_w)\n304\t                + (1.0 / eps_yy_n + 1.0 / eps_yy_s) / (2.0 * dy_n * dy_s)\n305\t                - k0**2\n306\t            )\n307\t\n308\t            # Hy block (diagonal coefficient for Hy equation)\n309\t            ayyp = (\n310\t                (1.0 / eps_yy_e + 1.0 / eps_yy_w) / (2.0 * dx_e * dx_w)\n311\t                + (1.0 / eps_xx_n + 1.0 / eps_xx_s) / (2.0 * dy_n * dy_s)\n312\t                - k0**2\n313\t            )\n314\t\n315\t            # Hx neighbors\n316\t            axxe = -(1.0 / eps_xx_e) / (dx_e * (dx_w + dx_e))  # West\n317\t            axxw = -(1.0 / eps_xx_w) / (dx_w * (dx_w + dx_e))  # East\n318\t            axxn = -(1.0 / eps_yy_n) / (dy_n * (dy_s + dy_n))  # South\n319\t            axxs = -(1.0 / eps_yy_s) / (dy_s * (dy_s + dy_n))  # North\n320\t\n321\t            # Hy neighbors\n322\t            ayye = -(1.0 / eps_yy_e) / (dx_e * (dx_w + dx_e))  # West\n323\t            ayyw = -(1.0 / eps_yy_w) / (dx_w * (dx_w + dx_e))  # East\n324\t            ayyn = -(1.0 / eps_xx_n) / (dy_n * (dy_s + dy_n))  # South\n325\t            ayys = -(1.0 / eps_xx_s) / (dy_s * (dy_s + dy_n))  # North\n326\t\n327\t            ix = i * ny + j\n328\t            iy = ix + N\n329\t\n330\t            # Apply BCs via direct modification of diagonal entries\n331\t            if j == ny - 1:\n332\t                if bc_north == 0:  # Dirichlet: Hx=0 at boundary\n333\t                    axxp += 2.0 * bc_north * axxs\n334\t                axxn += bc_north * axxs\n335\t                ayyp += bc_north * ayys\n336\t\n337\t            if j == 0:\n338\t                if bc_south == 0:\n339\t                    axxp += 2.0 * bc_south * axxn\n340\t                axxs += bc_south * axxn\n341\t                ayyp += bc_south * ayyn\n342\t\n343\t            if i == nx - 1:\n344\t                if bc_east == 0:\n345\t                    axxp += 2.0 * bc_east * axxe\n346\t                axxw += bc_east * axxe\n347\t                ayyp += bc_east * ayye\n348\t\n349\t            if i == 0:\n350\t                if bc_west == 0:\n351\t                    axxp += 2.0 * bc_west * axxw\n352\t                axxe += bc_west * axxw\n353\t                ayyp += bc_west * ayyw\n354\t\n355\t            # Assemble\n356\t            _add(ix, ix, axxp)\n357\t            _add(iy, iy, ayyp)\n358\t\n359\t            if j < ny - 1:\n360\t                _add(ix, i * ny + (j + 1), axxs)\n361\t                _add(iy, i * ny + (j + 1), ayys)\n362\t            if j > 0:\n363\t                _add(ix, i * ny + (j - 1), axxn)\n364\t                _add(iy, i * ny + (j - 1), ayyn)\n365\t            if i < nx - 1:\n366\t                _add(ix, (i + 1) * ny + j, axxe)\n367\t                _add(iy, (i + 1) * ny + j, ayye)\n368\t            if i > 0:\n369\t                _add(ix, (i - 1) * ny + j, axxw)\n370\t                _add(iy, (i - 1) * ny + j, ayyw)\n371\t\n372\t    A = sparse.csc_matrix((data, (rows, cols)), shape=(2 * N, 2 * N), dtype=np.float64)\n373\t    A.eliminate_zeros()\n374\t    return A\n375\t\n376\t\n377\tdef _reconstruct_hz(\n378\t    Hx: np.ndarray, Hy: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, beta: float\n379\t) -> np.ndarray:\n380\t    \"\"\"Reconstruct Hz from Hx and Hy using Maxwell's curl equation.\n381\t\n382\t    Hx and Hy are on staggered grids; Hz is defined at cell centers.\n383\t    We compute Hz using the curl of H:\n384\t        Hz[k,l] = (dHx/dy - dHy/dx) / (i*beta) at cell center (k,l)\n385\t    \"\"\"\n386\t    ny, nx = Hx.shape\n387\t    # Hz is defined at interior cell centers (ny-1, nx-1)\n388\t    Hz = np.zeros((ny - 1, nx - 1), dtype=np.complex128)\n389\t\n390\t    diffx = np.diff(x)\n391\t    diffy = np.diff(y)\n392\t\n393\t    # Valid range: j from 0 to ny-2, i from 0 to nx-2\n394\t    for j in range(ny - 1):\n395\t        for i in range(nx - 1):\n396\t            dx = diffx[i] if i < len(diffx) else diffx[-1] if len(diffx) > 0 else 1.0\n397\t            dy = diffy[j] if j < len(diffy) else diffy[-1] if len(diffy) > 0 else 1.0\n398\t\n399\t            # Average H at face centers\n400\t            Hx_j_i = Hx[j, i] if j < ny and i < nx else 0.0\n401\t            Hx_j1_i = Hx[j + 1, i] if j + 1 < ny and i < nx else 0.0\n402\t            Hx_j_i1 = Hx[j, i + 1] if j < ny and i + 1 < nx else 0.0\n403\t            Hx_j1_i1 = Hx[j + 1, i + 1] if j + 1 < ny and i + 1 < nx else 0.0\n404\t\n405\t            Hy_j_i = Hy[j, i] if j < ny and i < nx else 0.0\n406\t            Hy_j1_i = Hy[j + 1, i] if j + 1 < ny and i < nx else 0.0\n407\t            Hy_j_i1 = Hy[j, i + 1] if j < ny and i + 1 < nx else 0.0\n408\t            Hy_j1_i1 = Hy[j + 1, i + 1] if j + 1 < ny and i + 1 < nx else 0.0\n409\t\n410\t            dHxd_y = (Hx_j1_i1 + Hx_j1_i - Hx_j_i1 - Hx_j_i) / (2.0 * dy)\n411\t            dHyd_x = (Hy_j1_i1 + Hy_j1_i - Hy_j_i1 - Hy_j_i) / (2.0 * dx)\n412\t            Hz[j, i] = (dHxd_y - dHyd_x) / (1j * beta + 1e-30)\n413\t\n414\t    return Hz\n415\t\n416\t\n417\tdef _reconstruct_fields(\n418\t    Hx: np.ndarray,\n419\t    Hy: np.ndarray,\n420\t    Hz: np.ndarray,\n421\t    x: np.ndarray,\n422\t    y: np.ndarray,\n423\t    beta: float,\n424\t    omega: float,\n425\t    epsilon: EpsilonCallback,\n426\t) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:\n427\t    \"\"\"Reconstruct E fields from H fields using Maxwell's curl equations.\"\"\"\n428\t    ny, nx = Hx.shape\n429\t    diffx = np.diff(x)\n430\t    diffy = np.diff(y)\n431\t\n432\t    Ex = np.zeros((ny - 1, nx - 1), dtype=np.complex128)\n433\t    Ey = np.zeros((ny - 1, nx - 1), dtype=np.complex128)\n434\t    Ez = np.zeros((ny - 1, nx - 1), dtype=np.complex128)\n435\t\n436\t    for j in range(ny - 1):\n437\t        for i in range(nx - 1):\n438\t            dx = diffx[i] if i < len(diffx) else diffx[-1] if len(diffx) > 0 else 1.0\n439\t            dy = diffy[j] if j < len(diffy) else diffy[-1] if len(diffy) > 0 else 1.0\n440\t            xc = (x[j] + x[j + 1]) / 2.0 if j < len(x) - 1 else x[j]\n441\t            yc = (y[i] + y[i + 1]) / 2.0 if i < len(y) - 1 else y[i]\n442\t\n443\t            eps_xx, eps_xy, eps_yx, eps_yy, eps_zz = epsilon(xc, yc)\n444\t            det_eps = eps_xx * eps_yy - eps_xy * eps_yx + 1e-15\n445\t\n446\t            # dHz/dy and dHz/dx using safe indexing\n447\t            def safe_hz(jj, ii):\n448\t                if 0 <= jj < Hz.shape[0] and 0 <= ii < Hz.shape[1]:\n449\t                    return Hz[jj, ii]\n450\t                return 0.0\n451\t\n452\t            dHz_dy = (safe_hz(j, i) + safe_hz(j + 1, i) - safe_hz(j, i + 1) - safe_hz(j + 1, i + 1)) / (2.0 * dy)\n453\t            dHz_dx = (safe_hz(j + 1, i + 1) + safe_hz(j + 1, i) - safe_hz(j, i + 1) - safe_hz(j, i)) / (2.0 * dx)\n454\t\n455\t            # Average H at cell center\n456\t            def safe_h(jj, ii, arr):\n457\t                if 0 <= jj < ny and 0 <= ii < nx:\n458\t                    return arr[jj, ii]\n459\t                return 0.0\n460\t\n461\t            Hy_avg = (safe_h(j + 1, i + 1, Hy) + safe_h(j + 1, i, Hy) + safe_h(j, i + 1, Hy) + safe_h(j, i, Hy)) / 4.0\n462\t            Hx_avg = (safe_h(j + 1, i + 1, Hx) + safe_h(j + 1, i, Hx) + safe_h(j, i + 1, Hx) + safe_h(j, i, Hx)) / 4.0\n463\t\n464\t            # E = (1/(-iωε)) curl H\n465\t            Dx = 1j * (dHz_dy - 1j * beta * Hy_avg) / (omega + 1e-30)\n466\t            Dy = 1j * (1j * beta * Hx_avg - dHz_dx) / (omega + 1e-30)\n467\t\n468\t            Ex[j, i] = (eps_yy * Dx - eps_yx * Dy) / det_eps\n469\t            Ey[j, i] = (-eps_xy * Dx + eps_xx * Dy) / det_eps\n470\t            Ez[j, i] = 0.0\n471\t\n472\t    return Ex, Ey, Ez\n473\t\n474\t\n475\tdef solve_modes(\n476\t    config: ModeSolverConfig,\n477\t    epsilon: EpsilonCallback,\n478\t    x: tuple[float, ...],\n479\t    y: tuple[float, ...],\n480\t) -> tuple[ModeSolution, ...]:\n481\t    \"\"\"Solve for waveguide modes on a cross-sectional grid.\n482\t\n483\t    Args:\n484\t        config: Mode solver configuration\n485\t        epsilon: Callback returning permittivity tensor at (x, y)\n486\t        x: Cell-center x coordinates\n487\t        y: Cell-center y coordinates\n488\t\n489\t    Returns:\n490\t        Tuple of ModeSolution objects sorted by neff descending\n491\t    \"\"\"\n492\t    if eigs is None:\n493\t        raise ModuleNotFoundError(\"scipy is required for the mode solver\")\n494\t\n495\t    nx = len(x)\n496\t    ny = len(y)\n497\t    N = nx * ny\n498\t\n499\t    if N < 4:\n500\t        raise ValueError(f\"Grid too small: {nx} x {ny} cells; need at least 2x2\")\n501\t\n502\t    omega = 2.0 * math.pi / config.wavelength\n503\t    k = omega  # k₀ in the convention used\n504\t\n505\t    # Assemble sparse matrix\n506\t    A = assemble_mode_matrix(x, y, config.wavelength, epsilon, config.cross_section.boundaries)\n507\t\n508\t    # Target number of eigenvalues\n509\t    nev = min(config.mode_spec.num_modes, max(1, N // 4))\n510\t\n511\t    # Eigensolver sigma: target neff or None for largest real part\n512\t    sigma = None\n513\t    if config.mode_spec.target_neff is not None:\n514\t        sigma = config.mode_spec.target_neff**2 * k**2  # β² = neff² * k²\n515\t\n516\t    # The curl-curl operator is negative definite\n517\t    # So A·H = -β²·H, giving eigenvalues -β² < 0\n518\t    # We want the LARGEST algebraic eigenvalue (closest to zero)\n519\t    try:\n520\t        evals, evecs = eigs(\n521\t            A,\n522\t            k=nev + 5,  # Request extra to handle filtering\n523\t            sigma=sigma,\n524\t            tol=config.tolerance,\n525\t            which=\"LM\" if sigma is not None else \"SR\",  # Smallest Real when no sigma\n526\t            maxiter=2000,\n527\t        )\n528\t    except Exception as exc:\n529\t        raise RuntimeError(f\"eigensolver failed: {exc}\") from exc\n530\t\n531\t    modes: list[ModeSolution] = []\n532\t\n533\t    for idx in range(len(evals)):\n534\t        beta_sq = evals[idx]\n535\t\n536\t        # curl-curl gives -β², so β² = -eigenvalue\n537\t        # The eigenvalues should be negative for propagating modes\n538\t        if beta_sq.real >= 0:\n539\t            # Not a guided mode (would be radiating or evanescent)\n540\t            continue\n541\t\n542\t        beta_sq_neg = beta_sq.real  # eigenvalue of A (negative = -β²)\n543\t        beta_sq_positive = -beta_sq_neg  # this is β² > 0\n544\t\n545\t        if beta_sq_positive <= 0:\n546\t            continue\n547\t\n548\t        beta = math.sqrt(beta_sq_positive)\n549\t        neff = beta / k if k > 0 else 0.0\n550\t\n551\t        # Skip if neff is not in physical range\n552\t        if neff < 0.0 or neff > 10.0:\n553\t            continue\n554\t\n555\t        # Extract Hx, Hy\n556\t        Hx_flat = evecs[:N, idx]\n557\t        Hy_flat = evecs[N : 2 * N, idx]\n558\t\n559\t        Hx = Hx_flat.reshape((ny, nx))\n560\t        Hy epsilon, config.cross_section.boundaries)\n\n    # Target number of eigenvalues\n    nev = min(config.mode_spec.num_modes, max(1, N // 4))\n\n    # Eigensolver sigma: target neff or None for largest real part\n    sigma = None\n    if config.mode_spec.target_neff is not None:\n        sigma = config.mode_spec.target_neff**2 * k**2  # β² = neff² * k²\n\n    # The curl-curl operator is negative definite\n    # So A·H = -β²·H, giving eigenvalues -β² < 0\n    # We want the LARGEST algebraic eigenvalue (closest to zero)\n    try:\n        evals, evecs = eigs(\n            A,\n            k=nev + 5,  # Request extra to handle filtering\n            sigma=sigma,\n            tol=config.tolerance,\n            which=\"LM\" if sigma is not None else \"SR\",  # Smallest Real when no sigma\n            maxiter=2000,\n        )\n    except Exception as exc:\n        raise RuntimeError(f\"eigensolver failed: {exc}\") from exc\n\n    modes: list[ModeSolution] = []\n\n    for idx in range(len(evals)):\n        beta_sq = evals[idx]\n\n        # curl-curl gives -β², so β² = -eigenvalue\n        # The eigenvalues should be negative for propagating modes\n        if beta_sq.real >= 0:\n            # Not a guided mode (would be radiating or evanescent)\n            continue\n\n        beta_sq_neg = beta_sq.real  # eigenvalue of A (negative = -β²)\n        beta_sq_positive = -beta_sq_neg  # this is β² > 0\n\n        if beta_sq_positive <= 0:\n            continue\n\n        beta = math.sqrt(beta_sq_positive)\n        neff = beta / k if k > 0 else 0.0\n\n        # Skip if neff is not in physical range\n        if neff < 0.0 or neff > 10.0:\n            continue\n\n        # Extract Hx, Hy\n        Hx_flat = evecs[:N, idx]\n        Hy_flat = evecs[N : 2 * N, idx]\n\n        Hx = Hx_flat.reshape((ny, nx))\n        Hy = Hy_flat.reshape((ny, nx))\n\n        # Reconstruct Hz\n        Hz = _reconstruct_hz(Hx, Hy, np.asarray(x), np.asarray(y), beta)\n\n        # Reconstruct E fields\n        Ex, Ey, Ez = _reconstruct_fields(Hx, Hy, Hz, np.asarray(x), np.asarray(y), beta, omega, epsilon)\n\n        # Compute power normalization\n        power = float(\n            np.sum(np.abs(Ex) ** 2) + np.sum(np.abs(Ey) ** 2) + np.sum(np.abs(Ez) ** 2)\n        )\n        power_norm = 1.0 / math.sqrt(power) if power > 1e-15 else 1.0\n\n        def _to_tuple_complex(arr: np.ndarray) -> tuple[tuple[float, float], ...]:\n            flat = arr.flatten()\n            return tuple((float(v.real), float(v.imag)) for v in flat)\n\n        # Downsample H to cell centers\n        Hx_c = (Hx[:-1, :-1] + Hx[1:, :-1] + Hx[:-1, 1:] + Hx[1:, 1:]) / 4.0\n        Hy_c = (Hy[:-1, :-1] + Hy[1:, :-1] + Hy[:-1, 1:] + Hy[1:, 1:]) / 4.0\n        Hz_c = Hz\n\n        modes.append(\n            ModeSolution(\n                neff=neff,\n                wavelength=config.wavelength,\n                x=x,\n                y=y,\n                Ex=_to_tuple_complex(Ex * power_norm),\n                Ey=_to_tuple_complex(Ey * power_norm),\n                Ez=_to_tuple_complex(Ez * power_norm),\n                Hx=_to_tuple_complex(Hx_c * power_norm),\n                Hy=_to_tuple_complex(Hy_c * power_norm),\n                Hz=_to_tuple_complex(Hz_c * power_norm),\n                power=power * power_norm**2,\n            )\n        )\n\n        if len(modes) >= config.mode_spec.num_modes:\n            break\n\n    # Sort by neff descending\n    modes.sort(key=lambda m: -m.neff_real)\n    return tuple(modes)\n\n\n__all__ = [\n    \"EpsilonCallback\",\n using the equivalence principle to define the actual injected currents.\n219\t\n220\t     Notes\n221\t     -----\n222\t\n223\t        For the injection to work as expected (i.e. to reproduce the required ``E`` and ``H`` fields),\n224\t        the field data must decay by the edges of the source plane, or the source plane must span the entire\n225\t        simulation domain and the fields must match the simulation boundary conditions.\n226\t\n227\t        The equivalent source currents are fully defined by the field components tangential to the\n228\t        source plane. For e.g. source normal along ``z``, the normal components (``Ez`` and ``Hz``)\n229\t        can be provided but will have no effect on the results, and at least one of the tangential\n230\t        components has to be in the dataset, i.e. at least one of ``Ex``, ``Ey``, ``Hx``, and ``Hy``.\n231\t\n232\t        .. TODO add image here\n233\t\n234\t        ..\n235\t            TODO is this generic? Only the field components tangential to the custom source plane are needed and used\n236\t            in the simulation. Due to the equivalence principle, these fully define the currents that need to be\n237\t            injected. This is not to say that the normal components of the data (:math:`E_x`, :math:`H_x` in our example)\n238\t            is lost or not injected. It is merely not needed as it can be uniquely obtained using the tangential components.\n239\t\n240\t        ..\n241\t            TODO add example for this standalone\n242\t            Source data can be imported from file just as shown here, after the data is imported as a numpy array using\n243\t            standard numpy functions like loadtxt.\n244\t\n245\t        If the data is not coming from a ``tidy3d`` simulation, the normalization is likely going to be arbitrary and\n246\t        the directionality of the source will likely not be perfect, even if both the ``E`` and ``H`` fields are\n247\t        provided. An empty normalizing run may be needed to accurately normalize results.\n248\t\n249\t        To create this empty simulation it is recommended that users create a simulation with no structures but just a flux\n250\t        monitor (``tidy3D.FluxMonitor``) next to the custom source, ensuring that the flux monitor is at least one grid cell\n251\t        away from the source. Moreover, for accurate normalization, users must ensure that the same grid is used to run\n252\t        the original simulation as well as the empty simulation. The total flux calculated at the flux monitor of the empty\n253\t        simulation can then be used for proper normalization of results after ``tidy3d`` simulation.\n254\t\n255\t        The coordinates of all provided fields are assumed to be relative to the source center.\n256\t        In other words, the dataset is interpreted in a local coordinate frame centered at\n257\t        :attr:`center`; when injecting/interpolating, the simulation-space coordinates are\n258\t        ``dataset_coords + center``. This can be\n642\t        computed in our eigenmode solver :class:`tidy3d.plugins.mode.ModeSolver` and implement the mode simulation in\n643\t        FDTD.\n644\t\n645\t        Mode sources are normalized to inject exactly 1W of power at the central frequency.\n646\t\n647\t        The modal source allows you to do directional excitation. Illustrated\n648\t        by the image below, the field is perfectly launched to the right of the source and there's zero field to the\n649\t        left of the source. Now you can contrast the behavior of the modal source with that of a dipole source. If\n650\t        you just put a dipole into the waveguide, well, you see quite a bit different in the field distribution.\n651\t        First of all, the dipole source is not directional launching. It launches waves in both directions. The\n652\t        second is that the polarization of the dipole is set to selectively excite a TE mode. But it takes some\n653\t        propagation distance before the mode settles into a perfect TE mode profile. During this process,\n654\t        there is radiation into the substrate.\n655\t\n656\t        .. image:: /_static/img/mode_vs_dipole_source.png\n657\t\n658\t        **Practical Advice**\n659\t\n660\t        Place mode sources in waveguide sections with a uniform cross-section. The mode profile is\n661\t        computed assuming translational invariance (or constant bend radius) along the injection axis.\n662\t        For bent waveguides, set ``bend_radius`` and ``bend_axis`` accordingly. The pole-residue method \"\n        \"can be more accurate for highly dispersive modes and uses fewer broadband terms \"\n        \"than frequency samples.\",\n    )\n\n    @model_validator(mode=\"after\")\n    def _validate_num_freqs_limit(self) -> Self:\n        \"\"\"Enforce method-specific bounds on num_freqs.\"\"\"\n        if self.broadband_method == \"chebyshev\" and self.num_freqs > 20:\n            raise SetupError(\n                f\"For broadband_method='chebyshev', 'num_freqs' must be <= 20, got {self.num_freqs}.\"\n            )\n        if self.broadband_method == \"pole_residue\" and self.num_freqs < 3:\n            raise SetupError(\n                f\"For broadband_method='pole_residue', 'num_freqs' must be >= 3, got {self.num_freqs}. \"\n                \"The vector fitting algorithm requires more frequency samples than fit coefficients.\"\n            )\n        return self\n\n    @cached_property\n    def frequency_grid(self) -> NDArray:\n        \"\"\"Frequency grid used to approximate frequency dependence.\n\n        For Chebyshev: returns ``num_freqs`` Chebyshev-spaced points.\n        For pole_residue: returns ``num_freqs`` uniformly spaced points.\n        \"\"\"\n        if self.num_freqs == 1:\n            return np.array([self.source_time._freq0])\n        freq_min, freq_max = self.source_time.frequency_range_sigma(sigma=CHEB_GRID_WIDTH)\n        if self.broadband_method == \"pole_residue\":\n            return np.linspace(freq_min, freq_max, self.num_freqs)\n        return self._chebyshev_freq_grid(freq_min, freq_max)\n\n    def _chebyshev_freq_grid(self, freq_min: float, freq_max: float) -> NDArray:\n        \"\"\"A Chebyshev grid based on a minimum and maximum frequency.\"\"\"\n        freq_avg = 0.5 * (freq_min + freq_max)\n        freq_diff = 0.5 * (freq_max - freq_min)\n        uni_points = (2 * np.arange(self.num_freqs) + 1) / (2 * self.num_freqs)\n        cheb_points = np.cos(np.pi * np.flip(uni_points))\n        return freq_avg + freq_diff * cheb_points\n\n\n\"\"\" Source current profiles determined by user-supplied data on a plane.\"\"\"\n\n\nclass CustomFieldSource(FieldSource, PlanarSource):\n    \"\"\"Implements a source corresponding to an input dataset containing ``E`` and ``H`` fields,\n    using the equivalence principle to define the actual injected currents.\n\n     Notes\n     -----\n\n        For the injection to work as expected (i.e. to reproduce the required ``E`` and ``H`` fields),\n        the field data must decay by the edges of the source plane, or the source plane must span the entire\n        simulation domain and the fields must match the simulation boundary conditions.\n\n        The equivalent source currents are fully defined by the field components tangential to the\n        source plane. TODO add image here\n\n        ..\n            TODO is this generic? Only the field components tangential to the custom source plane are needed and used\n            in the simulation. Due to the equivalence principle, these fully define the currents that need to be\n            injected. This is not to say that the normal components of the data (:math:`E_x`, :math:`H_x` in our example)\n            is lost or not injected. It is merely not needed as it can be uniquely obtained using the tangential components.\n\n        ..\n            TODO add example for this standalone\n            Source data can be imported from file just as shown here, after the data is imported as a numpy array using\n            standard numpy functions like loadtxt.\n\n        If the data is not coming from a ``tidy3d`` simulation, the normalization is likely going to be arbitrary and\n        the directionality of the source will likely not be perfect, even if both the ``E`` and ``H`` fields are\n        provided. This can be\n        computed in our eigenmode solver :class:`tidy3d.plugins.mode.ModeSolver` and implement the mode simulation in\n        FDTD.\n\n        Mode sources are normalized to inject exactly 1W of power at the central frequency.\n\n        The modal source allows you to do directional excitation. Illustrated\n        by the image below, the field is perfectly launched to the right of the source and there's zero field to the\n        left of the source. Now you can contrast the behavior of the modal source with that of a dipole source. If\n        you just put a dipole into the waveguide, well, you see quite a bit different in the field distribution.\n        First of all, the dipole source is not directional launching. It launches waves in both directions. The\n        second is that the polarization of the dipole is set to selectively excite a TE mode. But it takes some\n        propagation distance before the mode settles into a perfect TE mode profile. During this process,\n        there is radiation into the substrate.\n\n        .. image:: /_static/img/mode_vs_dipole_source.png\n\n        **Practical Advice**\n\n        Place mode sources in waveguide sections with a uniform cross-section. The mode profile is\n        computed assuming translational invariance (or constant bend radius) along the injection axis.\n        For bent waveguides, set ``bend_radius`` and ``bend_axis`` accordingly. Avoid placing mode\n        sources at tapers, junctions, or other locations where the cross-section is changing.\n\n        .. TODO improve links to other APIs functionality here.\n\n    Example\n    -------\n    >>> from tidy3d import GaussianPulse\n    >>> pulse = GaussianPulse(freq0=200e12, fwidth=20e12)\n    >>> mode_spec = ModeSpec(target_neff=2.)\n    >>> mode_source = ModeSource(\n    ...     size=(10,10,0),\n    ...     source_time=pulse,\n    ...     mode_spec=mode_spec,\n    ...     mode_index=1,\n    ...     direction='-')\n\n    See Also\n    --------\n\n    :class:`tidy3d.plugins.mode.ModeSolver`:\n        Interface for solving electromagnetic eigenmodes in a 2D plane with translational invariance in the third dimension.\n\n    **Notebooks:**\n        * `Waveguide Y junction <../../notebooks/YJunction.html>`_\n        * `90 degree optical hybrid <../../notebooks/90OpticalHybrid.html>`_\n\n    **Lectures:**\n        * `Prelude to Integrated Photonics Simulation: Mode Injection <https://www.flexcompute.com/fdtd101/Lecture-4-Prelude-to-Integrated-Photonics-Simulation-Mode-Injection/>`_\n    \"\"\"\n\n    mode_index: NonNegativeInt = Field(\n        0,\n        title=\"Mode Index\",\n        description=\"Index into the collection of modes returned by mode solver. \"\n        \" Specifies which mode to inject using this source. \"\n        \"If larger than ``mode_spec.num_modes``, \"\n        \"``num_modes`` in the solver will be set to ``mode_index + 1``.\",\n    )\n\n\n\"\"\" Angled Field Sources one can use. \"\"\"\n\n\nclass AbstractAngularSpec(Tidy3dBaseModel, ABC):\n    \"\"\"Abstract base for defining angular variability specifications for plane waves.\"\"\"\n\n\nclass FixedInPlaneKSpec(AbstractAngularSpec):\n    \"\"\"Plane wave is injected such that its in-plane wavevector is constant. inject a plane wave in a finite region.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n\n        The TFSF source injects :math:`1 W` of power per :math:`\\\\mu m^2` of source area along the :attr:`injection_axis`.\n        Hence, the normalization for the incident field is :math:`|E_0|^2 = \\\\frac{2}{c\\\\epsilon_0}`, for any source size.\n        Note that in the case of angled incidence, the same power is injected along the source's :attr:`injection_axis`,\n        and not the propagation direction. This allows computing scattering and absorption cross-sections\n        without the need for additional normalization.\n\n        The TFSF source allows specifying a box region into which a plane wave is injected. Fields inside this region\n        can be interpreted as the superposition of the incident field and the scattered field due to any scatterers\n        present in the simulation domain. The fields at the edges of the TFSF box are modified at each time step such\n        that the incident field is cancelled out, so that all fields outside the TFSF box are scattered fields only.\n        This is useful in scenarios where one is interested in computing scattered fields only, for example when\n        computing scattered cross-sections of various objects.\n\n        It is important to note that when a non-uniform grid is used in the directions transverse to the\n        :attr:`injection_axis` of the TFSF source, the suppression of the incident field outside the TFSF box may not be as\n        close to zero as in the case of a uniform grid. Because of this, a warning may be issued when nonuniform grid\n        TFSF setup is detected. In some cases, however, the accuracy may be only weakly affected, and the warnings\n        can be ignored.\n\n    See Also\n    --------\n\n    **Notebooks**:\n        * `Defining a total-field scattered-field (TFSF) plane wave source <../../notebooks/TFSF.html>`_\n        * `Nanoparticle Scattering <../../notebooks/PlasmonicNanoparticle.html>`_: To force a uniform grid in the TFSF region and avoid the warnings, a mesh override structure can be used as illustrated here.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    num_freqs: int = Field(\n        1,\n        title=\"Number of Frequency Points\",\n        description=\"Number of points used to approximate the frequency dependence of the injected \"\n        \"field.
